C. Authorship of Scholarly Articles
The regulation at 8 C.F.R. § 214.2( o)(3)(iii)(B)( 6) requires the Petitioner to submit "[e]vidence of the
alien's authorship of scholarly articles in the field, in professional journals, or other major media."
The Petitioner argues that the Beneficiary has satisfied this criterion by submitting comparable
evidence showing that he has authored articles that are posted on his former employer's .l.. .______.
website as blog posts. See 8 C.F.R. § 214.2(o)(3)(iii)(C). The record includes three articles listing the
Beneficiary as an author. Two of them are one-page articles, and the remaining one is a two-page
article. Only one of the articles contains a "references" section. The Petitioner also offers materials
about I Iwebsite, indicating that it has a total of 440 pages, with 364 pages as blog posts,
including the Beneficiary's articles.
USCIS Policy Manual explains that "if a petitioner demonstrates that a particular criterion does not
readily apply to the beneficiary's occupation, the petitioner may submit evidence that is ofcomparable
significance to that criterion to establish sustained acclaim and recognition." See generally 2 USCIS
Policy Manual, supra, at M.4(C)(3). The Policy Manual farther provides the following example: "if
the publication of scholarly articles is not readily applicable to a beneficiary whose occupation is in
an industry rather than academia, a petitioner might demonstrate that the beneficiary's presentation of
work at a major trade show is of comparable significance to that criterion." Id.
Even if we assume that this criterion does not readily apply to the Beneficiary's occupation, the
Petitioner has not sufficiently demonstrated that the Beneficiary's authorship of these short articles is

of comparable significance as authorship of scholarly articles in professional journals, or other major
media, or of comparable significance as presentation of work at a major trade show. See 8 C.F.R.
§ 214.2(o)(3)(iii)(B)(6), (C); see generally 2 USCIS Policy Manual, supra, at M.4(C)(3). The

space."6 The documents, at best, indicate that the Beneficiary's former employer's website is one of
many resources people can visit if they want to learn more about artificial intelligence and machine
learning, or if they want to learn more about products that the Beneficiary's former employer offers.
They are, however, insufficient to confirm the website is comparable to a professional journal, other
major media, or a major trade show. Based on these reasons, the Petitioner has not demonstrated that
the Beneficiary satisfies this criterion, including through the submission of comparable evidence.

D. Critical or Essential Capacity
The regulation at 8 C.F.R. § 214.2( o) (3 )(iii)(B)( 7) requires the Petitioner to submit "[ e ]vidence that
the alien has been employed in a critical or essential capacity for organizations and establishments that
have a distinguished reputation." USCIS Policy Manual explains: "[r]elevant factors for evaluating
the reputation of an organization or establishment can include the scale ofits customer base, longevity,
or relevant media coverage." See generally 2 USCIS Policy Manual, supra, at M.4(C)(2).
Additionally, the Policy Manul states: "[f]or a startup business, [U.S. Citizenship and Immigration
Services (USCIS)] may consider evidence that the business has received significant funding from
government entities, venture capital funds, angel investors, or other such funders commensurate with
funding rounds generally achieved for that startup's stage and industry, as a positive factor regarding
its distinguished reputation." Id.

E. High Salary or Other Remuneration
The regulation at 8 C.F.R. § 214.2( o) (3 )(iii)(B)( 8) requires the Petitioner to submit "[ e ]vidence that
the alien has either commanded a high salary or will command a high salary or other remuneration for
services, evidenced by contracts or other reliable evidence." USCIS Policy Manual explains that under
certain circumstances, a petitioner may offer comparable evidence for this criterion, noting: "if the
petitioner demonstrates that receipt of a high salary is not readily applicable to the beneficiary's
position as an entrepreneur, the petitioner might present evidence that the beneficiary's highly valued
equity holdings in the startup are of comparable significance to the high salary criterion."
See generally 2 USCIS Policy Manual, supra, at M.4(C)(3).
